decks.title: Wikipedia Edit Stream
decks.summary_easy: A live browser dashboard that reads every edit to Wikipedia and its sister sites and counts it twice: exactly, and with three memory saving estimators (HyperLogLog, Count-Min, Space-Saving). Plotting the gap shows whether each estimator stays inside its promised error. On a 297 second run of 9,909 real events, the distinct editor estimate landed within 0.4% of the exact count.
decks.blurb: HyperLogLog, Count-Min, and Space-Saving run beside exact counters on the live Wikimedia event stream.

decks.title: Order Book Microstructure
decks.summary_easy: A live browser page that rebuilds Kraken's BTC/USD order book from a snapshot and about 142 updates a second, and checks it against the exchange's own checksum after every update, rebuilding from a fresh copy if a check ever fails. From that verified copy it measures how buying pressure moves the price and how volatile the price is. In a 330 second run all 46,892 checksums matched.
decks.blurb: A checksum verified live Kraken order book with spread, microprice, and order flow analytics.

decks.title: Live Earthquake Statistics
decks.summary_easy: A live browser dashboard on the US Geological Survey earthquake feed. It computes how much rarer big quakes are than small ones and how fast aftershocks fade, and it keeps a log of every correction USGS makes to its own catalog while the page is open. On October 8, 2026, California's b-value came out at 0.73 with a bootstrap range of 0.66 to 0.85.
decks.blurb: Gutenberg-Richter b-values, Omori decay, and a USGS catalog that revises itself while you watch.

decks.title: Space Weather Nowcast
decks.summary_easy: A live browser page that reads nine NOAA space weather feeds, follows the solar wind from a spacecraft 1.58 million km toward the Sun to Earth, and shows how hard it pushes on Earth's magnetic shield, the storm level, and the aurora chance over Syracuse. It was built as the live input side for Tanay's Kp forecasting model. On the measured run the wind was at 360 km/s and would reach Earth 73.5 minutes after it was measured.
decks.blurb: Nine NOAA feeds, solar wind propagated from L1 to Earth, and the aurora outlook over Syracuse.

decks.title: Replicating Dr. GRPO
decks.summary_easy: Tanay retrained Qwen2.5-1.5B on math problems with reinforcement learning, once with GRPO and once with Dr. GRPO, a 2025 fix that claims to stop wrong answers from getting longer without hurting accuracy. Using the paper's own data and grader, accuracy held (51.6% vs 51.2% on MATH500) but both length claims came out reversed. It is one seed and 100 short training steps, so Tanay reports it as not reproduced here rather than refuted.
decks.blurb: RL post training for math reasoning: the accuracy claim held and both length claims came out reversed.

decks.title: Tool Dependency Graph
decks.summary_easy: AI agents often fail because a tool needs an ID that only another tool can provide, like the thread ID needed to reply to an email. Tanay built a system that reads the schemas of 1,391 tools and maps which tools must run first and which inputs must come from the user. About two thirds of required inputs turn out to be handles another tool can supply, and almost all of those have a producer.
decks.blurb: Deriving agent call order from 1,391 tool schemas by static analysis.

decks.title: Distributed ViT on CIFAR-10
decks.summary_easy: Tanay trained a small image classification model on two GPUs and measured honestly what the second GPU bought. In full precision two GPUs were 1.96x faster than one; with mixed precision turned on, the same setup was only 1.15x faster. A controlled test showed the cause was a 4 core CPU host that could not prepare images fast enough, not the communication between GPUs.
decks.blurb: Proving a data parallel speedup, then explaining why it vanished.

decks.title: ZTF Transient Pipeline
decks.summary_easy: A nightly pipeline over real telescope alerts from the Zwicky Transient Facility: alerts are replayed through a Kafka broker, scored by a small image plus table classifier, and landed in a DuckDB warehouse, where dbt turns them into tested tables. Tanay ran it on 27,378 real alerts from July 20, 2026 and pushed 500 all the way through, with every dbt model and test passing. The plumbing and data contracts are real; the classifier is a smoke test model, not a science result.
decks.blurb: Real time astronomical alert classification on Kafka and Avro, with a dbt warehouse and drift checks.

decks.title: Groundwork
decks.summary_easy: Groundwork is a small AI question answering system over Wikipedia, built with the parts real products need and demos skip: measuring whether answers are right, refusing when it should, checking that safety filters do not block real users, and metering what each model call costs. On public data where half the questions have no answer, it correctly refuses 96.2% of those, and keyword search finds the right paragraph in the top five 92.1% of the time.
decks.blurb: RAG evaluation, guardrails, and an LLM gateway on real data.

decks.title: Replicating BEIR
decks.summary_easy: Tanay rebuilt the main experiment of BEIR, a benchmark showing that neural search models trained on one dataset often lose to plain keyword search on new kinds of documents. On two scientific datasets every published number he checked came back, and a newer 2023 model beat keyword search on both. The one number that first missed led him to a library default that silently cut every document to 100 tokens; fixing it matched the paper exactly.
decks.blurb: Reproducing a retrieval benchmark on one laptop and finding a silent truncation bug.

decks.title: ShopFloor AI
decks.summary_easy: ShopFloor AI predicts milling machine failures from five sensor readings, streams sensor KPIs and alerts through Kafka, and answers maintenance questions with a RAG assistant, all as one Docker Compose stack with MLflow and Airflow. On the synthetic AI4I 2020 dataset its gradient boosting model reached 0.85 F1 and 0.96 AUC. Reading the code back shows several connections between the parts that do not yet work as described, which Tanay owns as the main lesson.
decks.blurb: Predictive maintenance and RAG for the factory floor, served as a seven service stack.

decks.title: handoff
decks.summary_easy: handoff is a supervisor for incident response agents where every request for human approval has an owner, a deadline, and a rule written in advance for what happens if nobody answers. On silence it can drop the action, run a safer substitute, ask the next tier, or freeze, and it never treats silence as approval. It has 212 tests, 11 scenarios, and no dependencies, and it runs on a simulated cluster with rule based workers.
decks.blurb: Supervisor orchestration where every escalation carries an owner, a deadline, and a declared behavior for silence.

decks.title: comms-agent: Agent Orchestration for Communications Monitoring
decks.summary_easy: An agent that runs a weekly media monitoring job for a brand: it collects mentions, labels each for topic and tone, sends the uncertain ones to a person, and writes a short brief from the checked labels. It runs on a small synthetic sample with a stand in model and a simulated reviewer, because the point is the orchestration and the human review gate.
decks.blurb: Agent orchestration for communications monitoring.

decks.title: Project Mark
decks.summary_easy: Tanay built product analytics tasks on real, licensed data that were meant to make the strongest AI models fail while staying fair to a careful human: each had one correct business recommendation and a misleading but real headline number. They built and verified four trap families. On the most developed task, about student engagement data, frontier models rebuilt the analysis and answered correctly anyway, which Tanay reports as a calibrated negative result.
decks.blurb: Deterministic analytics traps that stress test frontier models.

decks.title: media-pulse: Communications Measurement with Review
decks.summary_easy: A communications measurement tool for a fictional brand: it labels each media mention for tone and topic with a confidence, sends the uncertain labels to a reviewer, and reports share of voice, key message pull through, and a quality check of the model itself. On a synthetic sample with a simulated reviewer, held out topic accuracy rose from 0.88 to 0.96 and sentiment from 0.50 to 0.85.
decks.blurb: Communications measurement with human in the loop QA.

decks.title: Multi Horizon Kp Prediction
decks.summary_easy: A four person course project that trained one LSTM neural network on NASA's hourly OMNI2 space weather data to forecast the Kp geomagnetic storm index 1, 3, 6 and 12 hours ahead. The reported 1 hour error was 0.738 Kp, 45% below always predicting the average, falling to about 10% better at 12 hours. The deck pairs those numbers with the weaknesses an interviewer will find: a weak baseline, an input that mirrors Kp, and a repo that cannot regenerate the results.
decks.blurb: Multi horizon deep learning forecasts of geomagnetic activity.

decks.title: The Perfect Lap: F1 Pit Stop Strategy
decks.summary_easy: A five person class project (IST 707, Team Omega) that predicts the lap on which a Formula 1 driver makes their first pit stop, from race length, circuit traits, grid slot, team, and year. A Random Forest landed about 2.78 laps from what teams actually did on a random holdout of driver race rows, and a Streamlit app wraps a lighter version of the model. The strongest interview material is what the evaluation missed and where the write up and the repo disagree.
decks.blurb: F1 pit stop strategy optimization with machine learning.

decks.title: July Energy Demand Under a Warming Climate
decks.summary_easy: A group project (IST 687, Jan to May 2025) for a South Carolina electricity provider: model how much electricity homes use each hour in July, then ask what a 5°C hotter July and a small thermostat change would do to demand. A Random Forest explained about half the variation (R² 0.48) and projected a 25.4% rise in the busiest evening hour under +5°C. A review of the code shows the thermostat savings figure is not isolated from the warming, which the deck explains.
decks.blurb: Predicting peak summer demand under a warming climate.

decks.title: Challenging "Wealth Equals Health"
decks.summary_easy: A data storytelling project in R on Gapminder data for 180+ countries from 2000 to 2020. Tanay tested whether national income predicts life expectancy (it does) and whether schooling still predicts child mortality once income is accounted for (it does), then wrote the result up for a non technical community audience as an argument for education investment in rural communities.
decks.blurb: Quantitative storytelling that finds education as the hidden lever.

decks.title: Uber Data Engineering Pipeline
decks.summary_easy: Tanay built the full path from raw New York City taxi trip data to an interactive Power BI dashboard on Google Cloud: a data lake in Cloud Storage, Python cleaning jobs on Compute Engine, a star schema loaded into partitioned BigQuery tables, and exploratory analysis in Jupyter. The goal was to do every stage of the data lifecycle once on real cloud services.
decks.blurb: An ETL pipeline and star schema for trip data.

decks.title: Travel Itinerary Management System
decks.summary_easy: Tanay designed the database behind a travel itinerary app: 12 normalized tables, 3 stored procedures, 2 triggers, and 1 function. The rules (no negative costs, no zero length activities, hotels tied to real destinations) are enforced by the database, so every app, import, or analyst gets the same guarantees, and a traveler's full itinerary is created in one all or nothing call.
decks.blurb: A normalized relational database for travel planning.

decks.title: Digit Recognition Neural Network from Scratch
decks.summary_easy: Tanay built a neural network that reads handwritten digits using only Python and NumPy, writing the forward pass, backpropagation, and training loop by hand. It reached 94% on the held out MNIST test set, and the real output was hands on experience with the classic training failures: bouncing and stalling losses, underfitting, and vanishing gradients.
decks.blurb: A neural network with hand written backpropagation.

decks.title: Big Data Inflow Delay Research
decks.blurb: Communication and computation delay across edge, fog, and cloud tiers.

decks.title: Gravity Spy 2.0 Research Assistant
decks.summary_easy: Tanay is a research assistant on Gravity Spy 2.0, an NSF funded citizen science project that helps LIGO find which detector hardware causes the noise bursts, called glitches, in gravitational wave data. Tanay built the pipeline that cleans more than 276,000 volunteer classifications and trained a neural network that predicts whether volunteers will call a sensor's signal similar to a glitch. The model ranks pairs well (0.89 AUC against volunteer labels), and its calibration error, the gap between its confidence and how often it is right, was cut in half, which matters more for how the scores will be used.
decks.blurb: LIGO glitch data: five schemas reconciled, 49,000 spectrograms, a calibrated two input CNN.

decks.title: JMA Wireless Lean Six Sigma Lead
decks.summary_easy: From January to May 2026, Tanay led a four person Lean Six Sigma team at JMA Wireless, a cell tower equipment maker, in the department that builds jumper cables. The team got five performance measures defined the same way for a manual line and an automated cell, built the data pipeline and dashboard, and found that the automated cell was almost never broken but was starved of parts. A daily standup Tanay piloted cut the time to act on a red measure from about four hours to about 25 minutes, and the projected value is about $355,000 a year pending the company's finance team.
decks.blurb: Five factory KPIs standardized, a 31 GB pipeline flattened, and the real constraint found upstream.

decks.title: ProProfs, Data and Product Analyst Intern
decks.blurb: Churn analysis, competitive benchmarking, and Tableau dashboards.

decks.title: Cybersecurity Teaching Assistant
decks.blurb: Security labs and environments, and the bridge to AI red teaming.

decks.title: How to narrate your work
decks.summary_easy: A course in talking about technical work out loud, built entirely from Tanay's own projects. It covers how long each answer should be, how to put numbers into spoken sentences, how to present results that reversed or vanished, and how to handle bugs, not knowing, pushback, AI tool questions and different audiences.
decks.blurb: The answer ladder, leading with the result, numbers with comparators, negative results, and pushback.

decks.title: Your story across the portfolio
decks.summary_easy: Ready to say answers for the questions that are about Tanay rather than about one project: tell me about yourself in three lengths for three kinds of role, walk me through your resume, which projects to lead with, what connects the work, and the full set of behavioral stories, each built from real projects with the numbers checked against the source.
decks.blurb: Tell me about yourself in three lengths and three framings, and every behavioral prompt mapped to a real project.
